plot_extraction.response_text:
Bored schoolboy William resents the vain, angelic-looking Evangeline after she is elected May Queen and he is made part of her court. He befriends shy, overlooked Bettine, who admires him and secretly longs to be queen. Learning that Evangeline is exceptionally greedy, William spends a gift of five shillings on cakes and lures her into his woodshed just before the May Day celebration, leaving her absorbed in eating them.

William then dresses Bettine in stolen fairy costume pieces and a tinsel crown, outfits himself as a makeshift May King, and leads her onto the May Queen’s platform. The dance begins before their stunned teacher can intervene, while the audience assumes William’s bizarre costume and moustache are part of the pageant. Bettine enjoys her triumphant moment as queen beside William, while Evangeline remains in the shed finishing the cakes.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story uses a brisk, polished comic style built around the contrast between an unruly child’s logic and the decorous assumptions of adults. The narration is third-person omniscient, but it remains closely aligned with William’s interests, resentments and schemes. It moves freely into brief accounts of other characters’ motives while treating William’s outlook as the story’s imaginative centre. The narrator’s voice is urbane, dry and knowingly ironic, often interpreting childish behaviour through the language of politics, military strategy or public affairs: William keeps his promise “with true political address,” Evangeline canvasses for votes, and his plans require “capital.” This mock-serious framing gives small schoolroom conflicts an exaggerated institutional importance.

The tone is affectionate but unsentimental. William is troublesome, vindictive and opportunistic, yet his audacity, inventiveness and loyalty to Bettine make him engaging rather than merely disobedient. The narrator rarely condemns him directly; instead, humour arises from understated observations, ironic qualifications and deadpan consequences. Hyperbole is frequent but controlled, as in Robert’s romantic despair, Jumble’s digestive suffering and Evangeline’s almost supernatural capacity for cakes. Parenthetical remarks and aphoristic statements—such as the warning that when something jars on William’s nerves, “something always happened”—create complicity between narrator and reader.

The prose alternates between compact narrative summary and extended dialogue scenes. Narrative sentences are generally clear and rhythmic, often using repetition for comic emphasis: William dislikes facts, detail and questions; Evangeline continues “eatin’ and eatin’ and eatin’”; Robert speaks of ruined life and happiness in accumulating clauses. Lists and parallel constructions heighten absurdity, particularly when cataloguing clothes, cakes, grievances or ceremonial instructions. Longer passages accelerate through coordination and repeated conjunctions, while short sentences or fragments provide punch lines. Deliberate anticlimax is common, with elevated phrasing collapsing into mundane objects such as bull’s-eyes, cold tongue, burnt cork or a currant cake.

Dialogue is central to characterization and is sharply differentiated from the narrator’s standard English. The children’s speech is represented through colloquial contractions and phonetic spellings—“goin’,” “jus’,” “narsy,” “wot,” “’Ullo”—along with simple syntax, repetition and literal-minded misunderstandings. William’s dialogue is blunt, argumentative and evasively ingenious. He exploits exact wording, as when he promises to write Evangeline’s name but invalidates the vote, and he habitually turns reluctance into ostensible virtue. Bettine speaks softly and earnestly, making her admiration emotionally direct. Evangeline’s simpering self-consciousness emerges through boastful remarks and affected sweetness. Adult speech, by contrast, is ceremonious, patronizing or melodramatic, and its failure to understand the children supplies much of the comedy.

Characterization depends on vivid recurring details rather than psychological exposition. William is defined by his scowl, untidiness, pockets full of miscellaneous objects, instinctive resistance to authority and theatrical taste for moustaches. Evangeline is reduced comically to blue clothes, ringlets, a squeaky voice and greed, while Bettine is small, dark, shy and generous. These motifs make the cast immediately legible and support the story’s fairy-tale opposition between the officially chosen “angel” and the overlooked child whom William crowns. Names such as Evangeline Fish and Bettine Franklin have a slightly caricatural crispness suited to the comic mode.

The plot is linear and carefully escalated. It begins with boredom and the May Queen election, develops William’s hostility and his friendship with Bettine, introduces the obstacle of his ceremonial role, then plants the crucial observation of Evangeline’s appetite. A comic family digression explains both William’s character and his temporary lack of money before the uncle’s five shillings provide the means for the scheme. Earlier details return as payoffs: the cakes become bait, Ethel’s costume becomes royal dress, and William’s insistence on a May King becomes reality. The climax depends on dramatic irony, since the reader understands William’s substitution while the audience tries to interpret it as an intentional pageant. The final sentence cuts back to Evangeline finishing the last cake, delivering a concise visual punch line rather than a moral or formal resolution.

The humour combines satire, incongruity, repetition and misunderstanding. School ceremonies, romantic ideals, feminine “mellowing,” beauty contests and adult respectability are all gently mocked. Adults repeatedly impose sentimental meanings on events they do not comprehend, while William pursues concrete desires with ruthless practicality. The story also reverses conventional values: the angelic blonde is vain and greedy, the supposedly disruptive boy performs an act of rough kindness, and the shabby substitute queen experiences genuine happiness. Sentiment is present in William and Bettine’s bond, but it is protected from mawkishness by comic gifts such as a half-eaten apple, a centipede and a crooked costume.

The setting is an idealized early twentieth-century English middle-class world of mixed schools, village festivals, servants, coal cellars, smocks and Maypole dances. Social customs are recognizable but lightly caricatured, and there is little descriptive atmosphere beyond what the action requires. Objects carry more stylistic weight than landscape: sweets, marbles, cakes, clothes and improvised props drive both characterization and plot. Overall, the style is economical, episodic and highly performative, combining an elegant adult narrator with vigorous child dialogue to turn minor rebellion into mock-heroic comedy.

## THE MAY KING

William was bored.

Boredom in William was not a passive condition. It was not the pale, drooping boredom of people who sit at windows and sigh. It was an active, dangerous force. When William was bored, doors slammed, ornaments fell, dogs fled, and adults began suddenly to inquire who had been meddling with things.

On this particular afternoon the schoolroom offered no legitimate outlet for his energies. Miss Milton was explaining the May Day celebrations.

“The election of the May Queen,” she said, smiling sentimentally over the rows of desks, “is an ancient and beautiful custom.”

William scowled.

He disliked ancient customs. They generally involved facts, dates, clean collars and standing still. He disliked beautiful customs even more. They generally involved girls.

“The child chosen,” Miss Milton continued, “should represent sweetness, grace and dignity.”

Every girl in the room sat suddenly upright and represented sweetness, grace and dignity.

William looked round in disgust.

Evangeline Fish represented them most conspicuously. She had pale-gold ringlets, large blue eyes and a blue sash. She generally wore blue. Her mother said it brought out the colour of her eyes. William considered that the colour of her eyes had been brought out quite far enough already.

Evangeline lowered her lashes.

“I shouldn’t like to be Queen,” she said in a squeaky little voice that could be heard in every corner of the room. “I’d be too shy.”

This was Evangeline’s opening move in the electoral campaign.

The election was to be conducted by ballot. Miss Milton distributed small squares of paper and instructed each child to write the name of the girl whom he or she considered most suitable.

“You must vote according to your conscience,” she said.

William had no high opinion of consciences. His own generally advised him to do things that grown-ups afterwards condemned. Still, he accepted the paper.

Evangeline turned round and smiled at him.

“You’ll write my name, won’t you, William?”

“No,” said William.

Her smile became sweeter.

“I know you will.”

“I won’t.”

“You promised you’d write my name.”

“I never did.”

“You did yesterday.”

William frowned. He remembered yesterday. Evangeline had offered him a bull’s-eye if he would write her name on the voting paper. William, wishing to obtain the bull’s-eye without entering into political controversy, had agreed to write it.

He took up his pencil.

Evangeline watched him.

Slowly and laboriously he wrote EVANGELINE FISH across the paper. Then, with true political address, he drew a thick line through it and wrote beneath:

BETTINE FRANKLIN.

“You said you’d write my name,” he whispered.

“You’ve crossed it out!”

“I never said I wouldn’t cross it out.”

Evangeline made a noise expressive of outrage, betrayal and the unexpected loss of public office.

Miss Milton looked up.

“Is anything wrong, Evangeline?”

“No, Miss Milton,” said Evangeline, with gentle fortitude. “It doesn’t matter.”

This was the second move in her campaign.

The papers were folded and collected. Miss Milton counted them, recounting twice because William’s paper contained so much pencil and because one elector had voted for the school cat.

At last she raised her hand.

“Evangeline Fish has been chosen May Queen by a large majority.”

Evangeline looked astonished. She had been preparing the astonishment for three days.

“Oh!” she squeaked. “Me?”

The girls clapped. Some of the boys clapped. William did not clap.

Bettine Franklin did. She was a small, dark child who sat at the end of the back row and was generally forgotten by everyone except the person collecting exercise books. Her hair was straight, her dress was brown, and her expression was one of shy expectation, as though life had promised her something but had not yet remembered what it was.

Evangeline stood while Miss Milton spoke about honour, responsibility and May blossoms. Evangeline’s ringlets trembled modestly. She glanced round to see whether everyone was looking at them.

William regarded her with growing dislike.

It was not merely that she had won. William could forgive victory if it were obtained by force, cunning or superior aim with a catapult. Evangeline had obtained it by smiles, ringlets, whispering, canvassing and the distribution of bull’s-eyes. She had won, in fact, by methods which William considered underhand.

Then came the blow.

“The Queen will have four attendants,” said Miss Milton, “and four pages. William Brown, Ginger, Douglas and Henry will be the pages.”

William stared at her.

“I’m not bein’ a page.”

“You are to have the honour of attending the May Queen.”

“I don’t want the honour.”

“You will wear a white blouse, green sash and a wreath of leaves.”

“I won’t.”

“And you will walk behind Evangeline carrying a garland.”

“I’ll be ill that day.”

Miss Milton smiled the smile with which adults acknowledge a child’s declaration of war.

“I’m sure you won’t, William.”

William looked at Evangeline. Evangeline smiled at him.

“I’ll try not to walk too fast for you,” she said kindly.

At that moment Evangeline’s fate was sealed. Nothing happened at once. Nothing ever did. William’s plans required time, material and an injustice large enough to sustain them. But when anything jarred upon William’s nerves so violently, something always happened in the end.

At recreation he found Bettine sitting alone beneath the chestnut tree.

“’Ullo,” he said.

“Hello, William.”

“Why did you vote for Evangeline?”

Bettine looked alarmed.

“Everyone did.”

“I didn’t.”

“Oh.”

“I voted for you.”

Her small face brightened.

“Did you really?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

William had not considered this. He kicked a stone.

“Dunno. You’re better’n her.”

“I’m not pretty.”

“You’re all right.”

This was not lavish praise, but Bettine received it as though a poet had addressed her beneath a balcony.

“I’d like to be Queen,” she admitted. “Not for always. Just for a little while. I’d like to wear a crown and sit up there where everyone could see me. But I wouldn’t be vain.”

“I know.”

“And I’d choose you for my page.”

“I wouldn’t be anyone’s page.”

“You could be King, then.”

William looked at her.

There was no May King in Miss Milton’s programme. This omission had already struck him as a grave defect. To William, a Queen without a King was not a ceremony but merely a girl showing off.

“Why isn’t there a May King?” he demanded later of Miss Milton.

“Because there isn’t,” said Miss Milton, who had been correcting arithmetic for forty minutes.

“There ought to be.”

“It is the custom to have a May Queen.”

“Well, it’s a silly custom.”

“William!”

“Kings are more important than Queens.”

“That is quite enough.”

“An’ I’m not bein’ a page.”

Miss Milton gave him extra arithmetic. Thus do governments answer constitutional criticism.

During the following week the May Day arrangements advanced. Garlands appeared, ribbons were measured, and Miss Milton rehearsed the children in a dance around a maypole erected on the village green. Evangeline attended every rehearsal wearing blue and issuing suggestions.

“I think the pages should walk more slowly,” she said.

“I think the Queen should shut up,” said William.

“William!”

“I only said—”

“I heard what you said.”

Evangeline practised ascending the platform. She practised smiling at the audience. She practised bowing to the Vicar’s wife. Once she tripped over her robe and blamed the nearest page, who happened to be William.

“You pushed me.”

“I never touched you.”

“You looked as if you were going to.”

Evangeline’s mother was making her a dress of white silk with forget-me-nots sewn round the hem. Reports of it circulated through the school like dispatches from a royal household.

Meanwhile Bettine remained at the back of everything. She was not an attendant because her dress was unsuitable, and she was not in the first dancing circle because she was small. She watched Evangeline’s rehearsals with admiration unspoilt by envy.

William had begun to share his treasures with her. He gave her a green marble, a dead beetle in a matchbox, half an apple and a centipede which escaped before she could take it home. Bettine accepted each gift gravely. In return she gave him a pencil, two bits of string and unlimited admiration.

This friendship caused some surprise in William’s family.

“William seems to be mellowing,” said Mrs Brown.

“Mellowing?” said Robert gloomily. “No one mellows. People pretend to mellow, and then they ruin your life.”

Robert had lately suffered an emotional disaster. A girl called Celia had danced twice with a man in a grey suit, and Robert’s faith in women, happiness and civilization had collapsed.

“You don’t understand,” he told his mother. “When one has built one’s entire existence upon a single perfect trust, and then sees it shattered—utterly shattered—before one’s eyes—”

“You’ve dropped marmalade on the tablecloth,” said Mrs Brown.

Robert stared into the distance.

“What does marmalade matter when life itself—?”

“It matters to me. Please wipe it up.”

Robert wiped it up with the air of a man signing away his ancestral estates.

Ethel, William’s elder sister, was preparing for a fairy play at the Women’s Institute. She had a silver wand, gauze wings, a rose-coloured tunic and a starry head-dress. These objects lay in her room under strict prohibition.

William had examined them all.

He had also found in the box-room an old black jacket belonging to Robert, a pair of scarlet curtains, a cardboard shield and a quantity of tinsel left from Christmas. At the time he had no settled purpose. William often collected information before events supplied it with meaning.

The chief difficulty was money.

William’s ordinary capital consisted of three halfpence, a foreign coin, two buttons and a tram ticket. He could sometimes negotiate with Ginger, but Ginger’s resources were little better. Douglas had sixpence, but intended to buy a whistle. Henry had nothing except a white mouse and would not sell it.

Then Uncle Frederick came to tea.

Uncle Frederick was stout, prosperous and fond of children from a safe distance. He arrived in a motor-car, pinched Ethel’s cheek, asked Robert whether he was breaking hearts yet, and slapped William on the shoulder with enough heartiness to cause permanent resentment.

“Well, young scamp,” he said, “and what do you want to be when you grow up?”

“Nothin’,” said William.

“Ha! Ha! A gentleman of leisure, eh?”

William did not know what a gentleman of leisure was, but suspected it of being insulting.

At tea Uncle Frederick talked of business, taxation, golf and the decline of modern manners. Jumble, William’s mongrel, sat beneath the table and received in rapid succession a piece of cake, two sardines, a lump of cold tongue and a sugared almond. The contributions came from different people, each believing himself alone in generosity. Jumble accepted them all with the fatal politeness of his kind.

After tea Uncle Frederick prepared to leave.

“Here, my boy,” he said. “Buy yourself something useful.”

He gave William five shillings.

Five shillings!

William stared at it. Never before had wealth in such solid and splendid form entered his possession. Five shillings meant sweets, fireworks, catapult elastic, a mouth-organ and still perhaps enough left for another mouth-organ when the first was confiscated.

Mrs Brown intervened.

“You must put it in your money-box, dear.”

William closed his hand over it.

“I’ll put it somewhere safe.”

His pocket was somewhere, and it was as safe as any place whose contents included a penknife without a handle, two acorns, a bent nail and a piece of treacle paper.

That evening Jumble was ill.

He lay beneath the kitchen table looking reproachfully at mankind. His sufferings were various and audible.

“I can’t think what he’s eaten,” said Mrs Brown.

William could. William had given him the sugared almond.

The family discussed Jumble’s digestion, Robert’s ruined life and Ethel’s fairy costume. William sat silent. He had suddenly remembered something.

That afternoon, after rehearsal, he had seen Evangeline enter the baker’s shop with a shilling her mother had given her for ribbon. She had emerged ten minutes later without ribbon, but eating a cream bun. She had then eaten a jam tart, two sponge fingers and a macaroon while walking home. She had eaten steadily, secretly and with remarkable concentration.

The next day he tested his discovery.

“Want a bit of cake?” he said to her at recreation.

“What sort?”

“Currant.”

“I don’t mind.”

She ate it.

“Thought you didn’t like currants.”

“I don’t, really,” said Evangeline, licking a crumb from her finger.

On the following day he offered her a stale ginger biscuit which he had found in his pocket.

She ate that too.

William considered the matter. Evangeline was vain, deceitful and squeaky, but these qualities were merely irritating. Her appetite was strategic.

On the morning of May Day, William went alone to the baker’s shop.

He bought two cream buns, four jam tarts, six sponge cakes, three macaroons, a currant cake, a bag of meringues, two iced buns, half a pound of biscuits and a small cake bearing the word WELCOME in pink sugar. The baker, accustomed to small purchasers of one halfpenny sweet, regarded him with respect.

William carried the parcel home by a circuitous route and concealed it in the woodshed behind the coal scuttle.

He then inspected the other materials of his campaign.

Ethel and Mrs Brown had gone early to help decorate the tea marquee. Robert had gone for a walk in order to recover, if possible, from love. The housemaid was upstairs. William entered Ethel’s room.

He took the rose-coloured tunic, the gauze wings and the silver wand. After reflection he left the starry head-dress because it would not fit Bettine and substituted a narrow band of tinsel fastened to cardboard points. It was a crown of simple but effective construction.

From Robert’s room he took the old black jacket. From the box-room he took the scarlet curtains and the cardboard shield. From the kitchen he took a burnt cork.

The burnt cork was important.

At half-past one the village green was bright with flags, white dresses, straw hats and adults congratulating one another upon the weather. The maypole stood in the centre with coloured ribbons hanging from it. A flower-covered platform had been built beside the tea marquee. On this Evangeline was to be crowned at two o’clock.

Evangeline arrived at one-thirty in white silk, forget-me-nots and ringlets. Her mother walked beside her carrying a cloak and looking as if she had personally arranged the month of May.

“You look quite angelic, darling,” said Miss Milton.

Evangeline lowered her eyes.

“I feel so frightened,” she squeaked.

She was not frightened. She had spent the morning practising a royal wave before the looking-glass.

William, wearing his ordinary clothes and a forbidding expression, approached her.

“Got something to show you.”

“I’ve no time. I’m the Queen.”

“It’s cakes.”

Evangeline hesitated.

“What cakes?”

“Lots.”

“I’ve had my lunch.”

“All right,” said William, turning away.

“Where are they?”

“In our woodshed.”

“Why?”

“’Cause I put ’em there.”

“I oughtn’t to go. Mummy said I mustn’t get my dress dirty.”

“They’re wrapped up.”

“What sort are they?”

William began the catalogue. At the second cream bun Evangeline glanced towards her mother. At the first macaroon she took one step after him. At the WELCOME cake she surrendered.

“I’ll only look,” she said.

“Please yourself.”

They slipped from the green by the lane and entered the Browns’ garden through a gap in the hedge. William opened the woodshed.

The cakes lay upon an upturned packing-case. Seen together they possessed a grandeur beyond their price. The meringues shone. The jam tarts glowed. WELCOME smiled pinkly upon the world.

Evangeline drew in her breath.

“They’re for the celebration,” said William. “But they won’t miss a few.”

“Are they really?”

“Yes.”

This was untrue, but William’s scheme had reached a point at which truth was no longer practical.

Evangeline sat on a box. She took a cream bun.

“You won’t tell?”

“No.”

William shut the door, leaving it unlatched.

He did not lock her in. This was partly because the lock was broken and partly because he understood Evangeline. No prison constructed by man could have held her more securely than those cakes.

At a quarter to two William found Bettine behind the tea marquee.

She wore her brown dress and was carrying a tray of paper napkins for Miss Milton.

“Come on,” he said.

“Where?”

“You’re goin’ to be Queen.”

Bettine stared at him.

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

“But Evangeline—”

“She’s busy.”

“What with?”

“Government business.”

He led Bettine through the hedge and up to Ethel’s room. There he explained the plan with the brevity of a commander whose troops need confidence rather than details.

Bettine turned pale.

“Miss Milton’ll be angry.”

“She’s always angry.”

“My mother’ll be angry.”

“She won’t till afterwards.”

This distinction reassured her slightly.

William pulled the fairy tunic over her brown dress. It hung crookedly, one wing pointing upwards and the other down. He fastened the scarlet curtain round her shoulders and placed the tinsel crown upon her dark hair.

Bettine looked at herself in the glass.

For one moment she said nothing.

“Oh, William,” she whispered. “I do look like a Queen.”

“You look better’n Evangeline.”

This was William’s sincere opinion. Bettine had none of Evangeline’s finish, but she had ceased to be shy. Her eyes shone, her cheeks were flushed, and the bent crown had altered her entire relation to the world.

William then dressed himself.

Robert’s black jacket reached nearly to his knees. He tied the second scarlet curtain round his waist, hung the cardboard shield from his neck and made a crown from a strip of gold paper. Last, with burnt cork, he drew a heavy moustache across his upper lip.

The effect was not conventional royalty. It suggested a pirate who had recently inherited a Balkan principality. William was satisfied.

“A King ought to have a sword,” he said.

He took the poker.

They returned by the hedge.

At five minutes past two Miss Milton was becoming anxious.

“Where is Evangeline?”

No one knew.

“Where is William?”

No one knew this either, but less anxiety was felt.

Evangeline’s mother searched the marquee. Miss Milton searched behind the platform. The Vicar’s wife looked at her watch. The musicians, under the impression that everything was ready, raised their instruments.

Then William and Bettine appeared.

They came through the crowd hand in hand. Bettine’s gauze wings trembled behind her. Her scarlet cloak dragged over the grass. William marched beside her, moustached, crowned, shielded and carrying the poker upright.

The audience became silent.

Adults are slow to believe in disaster when bunting is present. For several seconds everyone assumed that this extraordinary entrance formed part of the entertainment.

“How original,” murmured the Vicar’s wife.

“Some sort of allegory,” said the Vicar.

“I expect he represents Spring,” said a lady in mauve.

William mounted the flower-covered platform. He helped Bettine up after him and seated her upon Evangeline’s throne.

Miss Milton recovered the use of her limbs.

“William!”

At that instant the band began.

The children, drilled for weeks to move when the music started, moved. The attendants formed their circle. The pages took up the garland. Ginger, seeing William upon the platform in a moustache, nearly dropped his end, but discipline prevailed. The dancers caught the ribbons and began to weave them round the pole.

Miss Milton could not stop the dance without crossing the ring, upsetting the children and publicly admitting that she had no idea what was happening. She stood at the edge of the green, smiling with desperate brightness.

William raised the poker in salute.

The audience applauded.

Encouraged, he bowed. The cardboard shield struck his knees. His gold-paper crown slipped over one eye. He pushed it back and assumed an expression of ferocious majesty.

Bettine sat very still.

She had never before been watched by so many people. Usually, if people looked in her direction, it was because someone more important stood behind her. Now the music circled her, the ribbons flashed round the pole, and a hundred faces smiled up at her. She lifted one hand and waved.

The audience applauded again.

“She’s charming,” said the Vicar’s wife.

“Such a natural little thing,” said the lady in mauve.

“Far sweeter than the fair child who was to have done it,” whispered someone who had not been introduced to Evangeline’s mother.

Bettine heard the applause. Her crown was crooked, her wing was tearing, and William’s scarlet drapery had begun to come undone; but she was Queen.

William looked at her and grinned beneath his moustache.

“Like it?” he whispered.

“Oh, yes.”

The dancers completed their final turn and bowed. William stepped forward.

He had intended to make a speech, but had prepared only its opening.

“Ladies an’ gentlemen,” he said loudly, “this is the May Queen, an’ I’m the May King, ’cause there ought to be one.”

There was a pause.

Then a man at the back laughed. Others joined him. The applause became tremendous. The audience believed the speech to be a carefully designed piece of childish comedy.

Miss Milton did not.

“Come down at once,” she said through a fixed smile.

William, seeing no advantage in remaining after the triumph, helped Bettine from the throne. They descended amid cheers.

Bettine’s mother reached them first. She stared at the tunic, the wings and the tinsel crown.

“Bettine! What have you done?”

Bettine looked up at her, still radiant.

“I’ve been Queen.”

This was undeniable. Even her mother could not immediately discover an answer to it.

Then Ethel arrived.

“My costume!”

Robert arrived behind her.

“My jacket!”

Mrs Brown arrived behind Robert.

“William!”

Miss Milton came from the other direction.

“Where is Evangeline?”

Four accusations, each serious in itself, converged upon William. He stood with his crown over one eye, his moustache smeared across his cheek and the poker in his hand.

He considered retreat.

At that moment Evangeline’s mother screamed from the edge of the green.

“Evangeline!”

Everyone turned.

Evangeline was approaching slowly through the hedge. Her white silk dress bore jam upon the front, cream upon one sleeve and crumbs in every fold. One forget-me-not hung from a ringlet. She carried the remains of the WELCOME cake in both hands and was eating it as she came.

She had eaten the cream buns, the jam tarts, the sponge cakes, the macaroons, the meringues, the iced buns, the biscuits and most of the currant cake. She had heard the distant music. She had heard the applause. But there had always been one more cake.

“What have you been doing?” cried her mother.

Evangeline stopped.

She looked at the empty throne, at Bettine’s crown, at William’s moustache and at the crowd staring at her.

Then she looked down at the cake.

There was one sugared pink letter left upon it.

Evangeline ate it.

### The Cartographer of Lost Roads

On the morning the road disappeared, Mara Venn was painting a river that no longer existed.

She sat at her narrow desk beneath the eastern window of the Royal Map Room, bent over a sheet of calfskin. With a brush made from three squirrel hairs, she drew a line of blue through the kingdom’s western hills. The river had dried before Mara was born, but the king’s oldest maps showed it running broad and silver from the mountains to the sea.

“Leave it out,” said Master Orin, passing behind her.

Mara lifted her brush. “But it was there.”

“Was,” Orin replied. “Maps are for finding what is, not mourning what was.”

He continued between the desks, his black robe whispering across the tiles.

Mara looked again at the thin blue line. Then, with a cloth, she pressed gently until the river blurred and vanished.

At noon, a messenger arrived covered in chalk dust. He carried a leather tube sealed with red wax and insisted on giving it directly to Master Orin. Within minutes, every cartographer had been called to the central table.

Orin unrolled the document. It was a survey map of the North Road, the royal highway linking the capital to seven villages and the fortress at Bellweather Pass.

A jagged black mark crossed it.

“The road is gone,” said the messenger.

Nobody laughed.

Roads could flood, collapse, become overgrown, or be destroyed by war. They did not simply disappear.

“What do you mean, gone?” Orin asked.

“I mean that yesterday it led from Millgate to Bracken Ford. This morning it stopped at the thirty-third mile. Beyond that there is grass. Old grass, sir. Oaks growing where the road should be.”

Master Orin frowned. “And from the northern side?”

“A rider came down from Bellweather. The road ends there too.”

The cartographers gathered closer.

“What lies between the two ends?” Mara asked.

The messenger turned toward her. “No one knows.”

“Villages lie between them,” said Orin. “Farms. Bridges. Three inns.”

The messenger swallowed. “No one we’ve asked remembers any villages.”

Silence spread across the Map Room.

Mara felt something cold move along her spine. She looked toward the western wall, where the kingdom’s largest map hung from ceiling to floor. Mountains rose in brown ink, forests in green, towns in red. The North Road ran like a pale ribbon through the upper provinces.

Except now it ended thirty-three miles from the capital.

Beyond it lay an empty patch of parchment.

Master Orin saw it too.

All day, they searched the archives. Maps were pulled from cabinets and unrolled across floors. Dust rose in golden clouds. On every new map, the North Road ended at the same point. Only the oldest charts showed it continuing through places called Alderhook, Saint Lume, and Quiet Valley.

Mara found a census ledger mentioning four thousand people in the vanished region. The next time she opened it, the pages were blank.

By sunset, Master Orin locked the doors.

“No one leaves,” he announced. “Memory is changing with the records. We must write down what we know before it is taken.”

They worked through the night, copying names from fading documents. Yet the ink vanished almost as soon as it dried. One by one, the cartographers began to forget why they were writing.

At midnight, Mara found herself staring at a list in her own hand.

ALDERHOOK  
SAINT LUME  
QUIET VALLEY  
THE LANTERN INN  
BRACKEN FORD

The names meant nothing to her.

She was about to throw the page away when she noticed a note at the bottom.

Remember your brother.

Mara gripped the table.

She had a brother.

The knowledge came not as a memory but as an absence shaped like one. A chair at the family table. A second pair of boots beside the door. Someone laughing as he chased her through wet grass.

Then his name returned.

Jonas.

He had left the capital six years ago to repair the bells at Saint Lume.

Mara pressed both hands to her mouth.

How could she have forgotten him?

She ran to the western wall. The great map showed nothing beyond the broken road, only pale parchment marked with the words UNSURVEYED LAND.

Master Orin stood behind her.

“What are you doing?” he asked.

“My brother is there.”

“There is no ‘there.’”

“There was yesterday.”

Orin’s face tightened. For an instant, recognition flickered in his eyes. “My wife,” he whispered.

Mara turned.

“She went north last spring,” he said. “To visit her sister.”

He sank into a chair. Around them, other cartographers were discovering their own losses. An apprentice remembered a grandmother. A colorist recalled buying apples from a farmer on the North Road. The messenger began to weep because he suddenly knew he had been born in a village that no longer existed.

“What can erase land?” Mara asked.

Orin looked at the oldest map on the table. Its edges were burned, and the ink had faded to brown. In the vanished region, beside a drawing of a tower, someone had written a single word:

Nemor.

“The first royal cartographer,” Orin said. “He mapped the kingdom after the Wars of Division. According to legend, he discovered that roads are more than stone and dirt. A true road exists because people agree that one place may lead to another.”

Mara stared at him.

“Maps strengthen that agreement,” he continued. “They bind distance to memory. Nemor believed that if a map could preserve a road, another kind of map could destroy one.”

“Why would anyone do that?”

“To hide something. Or protect it.”

A bell rang outside, announcing one in the morning.

On the table, Saint Lume faded from the oldest map.

Mara reached for a blank sheet. “Then we draw it back.”

Orin shook his head. “We no longer know where it belongs.”

“My brother knows.”

“If your brother still exists.”

“He does.”

“How can you be certain?”

Mara thought of the empty chair, the boots by the door, and laughter in the rain.

“Because forgetting him hurts.”

Before dawn, she packed ink, quills, measuring cord, a compass, three days’ food, and the oldest map. Master Orin tried to stop her, but when she asked whether he wanted his wife left in blank parchment, he gave her his horse.

“Do not trust the landscape,” he warned. “A place being erased will defend its emptiness.”

The broken road lay half a day north of the capital.

Mara reached it under a gray sky. One moment, the horse’s hooves struck white stones. The next, they stepped onto grass.

The road ended in a perfect line.

Beyond it stood an ancient forest.

The messenger had spoken truly. The trees were enormous. Their roots twisted through dark soil undisturbed by wheel or foot. No road had ever passed between them.

Yet Mara remembered traveling north as a child. She and Jonas had ridden in their father’s cart, counting milestones. There had been no forest—only wheat fields, cottages, and a hilltop chapel with a copper roof.

She dismounted and opened the oldest map.

The North Road was fading from it even as she watched.

Mara dipped her quill and traced the line again. “From Millgate,” she said aloud, “the road runs north by northwest.”

The fresh ink gleamed.

The forest shuddered.

A narrow path appeared between the trees.

Mara led the horse forward. Behind her, the path vanished.

For hours, she advanced by drawing. Whenever the way disappeared, she added another line to the map. Sometimes the forest gave way to cliffs, marshes, or fields of black stone. She measured distances, checked the compass, and trusted the old chart more than her eyes.

Near evening, she came upon a milestone half buried in moss.

MILLGATE 41  
ALDERHOOK 3

The name stirred a faint memory. Alderhook had been famous for pears. Jonas once sent her a basket of them, each fruit wrapped in newspaper.

Mara drew a circle where the village should be.

The trees folded backward like curtains.

Houses appeared.

They stood along an empty road beneath a violet sky. Smoke hung motionless above chimneys. Doors were open. A dog was frozen in the act of crossing a yard, one paw raised. Beside a well, a woman leaned over a bucket, perfectly still.

Mara approached her.

“Can you hear me?”

The woman did not blink.

Mara touched her sleeve. The cloth was warm.

They had not been erased, she realized. They had been removed from time.

She unfolded the map on the well and carefully wrote ALDERHOOK in black ink.

The dog’s paw struck the ground.

The bucket splashed into the well.

The woman gasped and stumbled backward. Then every sound in the village arrived at once: axes striking wood, babies crying, doors closing, someone singing inside a house.

The woman stared at Mara. “Who are you?”

“Mara Venn, of the Royal Map Room. How long have you been standing here?”

“Standing where?”

“By the well.”

“I only just came for water.”

Mara looked at the sky. “What day is it?”

The woman answered.

It was yesterday.

A crowd gathered while Mara explained as much as she understood. Most people did not believe her until they tried to leave and found the forest waiting at both ends of the village.

An old innkeeper pushed through the crowd.

“It’s the tower,” he said.

Mara showed him the symbol on the ancient map.

His face went pale. “Nemor’s Watch. No one goes there.”

“Why?”

“Because it was built to be forgotten.”

The innkeeper told her an old story. After the Wars of Division, the defeated princes had hidden a weapon in the northern hills. Not a sword or cannon, but a book containing the true names of every road in the kingdom. Whoever possessed it could isolate cities, divide armies, or erase the path to a king’s door.

Nemor had sealed the book inside his tower. Then he removed the tower from all maps, hoping it would vanish from human memory.

“But someone found it,” Mara said.

The innkeeper nodded. “Or the book found someone.”

She left the horse in Alderhook and continued on foot. The restored villagers promised to keep writing their village’s name on every wall, door, and scrap of paper.

The road to Saint Lume fought her.

Rain fell upward. Hills changed places when she looked away. Her compass pointed toward her own chest. Once, she walked for an hour only to pass the same dead fox three times.

So Mara began mapping more than the land.

Beside a stone bridge, she wrote: Here Mara Venn was afraid, but continued.

At a fork in the road: The left path smells of pine. The right smells of snow. Choose the snow.

Near midnight: Jonas taught Mara to whistle with two fingers. She never learned.

The personal notes held firm when distances did not. They became nails driven into the shifting world.

At dawn, she found Saint Lume.

The town surrounded a white chapel with twin bell towers. Like Alderhook, it was frozen. Birds hung in the air. A bell waited above the town, caught between one chime and the next.

Mara wrote the town’s name.

Sound crashed over her.

The great bell completed its swing.

Jonas stood beneath it.

He was older than she remembered, broad-shouldered, with copper dust in his beard. He held a hammer in one hand.

Mara climbed the tower stairs so quickly that she nearly fell. She struck him with both arms and held on.

He laughed in surprise. “Mara? What are you doing here?”

She could not answer for a while.

When she finally explained, Jonas listened without interruption.

“I knew something was wrong with the bells,” he said. “Yesterday they began ringing backward.”

“Backward?”

“Each note arrived before the hammer struck. Then a stranger came to the chapel. A thin man in a gray coat. He asked for directions to Nemor’s Watch.”

“You told him?”

“I told him the tower was a children’s tale. He said children’s tales are maps drawn in words.”

Jonas led her to the chapel door. Scratched into the wood was a symbol: a circle divided by a crooked line.

Mara recognized it as the mark on the messenger’s survey.

“He went north,” Jonas said. “I’ll come with you.”

“No.”

“You crossed a vanishing country to find me, and now you expect me to stay behind?”

“I expect you to keep Saint Lume on the map.”

She gave him paper and ink. “Write everything you remember. Roads, houses, people. Make copies. Send riders south if the way opens.”

Jonas understood. Maps were not only lines and borders. They were acts of witness.

Before she left, he handed her a small brass bell.

“For finding your way back,” he said.

Beyond Saint Lume, the road climbed into snow.

By noon, Mara saw Nemor’s Watch.

The tower stood upside down above a frozen lake, its foundations buried in the clouds and its pointed roof touching the ice. A door waited at the base of the roof.

Mara crossed the lake. With each step, cracks spread beneath her boots, revealing not water but glimpses of other places: a summer orchard, a burning city, her childhood bedroom, Master Orin sitting alone in the Map Room.

At the door, the man in gray was waiting.

He was thin, as Jonas had said, but not old. His eyes were colorless.

“You took longer than I expected,” he said.

“Who are you?”

“Edrin Vale. Assistant Archivist, Third Chamber.”

Mara remembered seeing him in the palace archives, always carrying keys.

“Why did you erase the road?”

“I erased nothing. I merely opened the book.”

He stepped aside.

Inside the tower, stairs rose downward. Mara followed them into a circular room where thousands of maps covered the walls. At the center stood a stone pedestal and, upon it, a book bound in white leather.

It was open.

Words moved across its pages like insects.

Edrin approached it reverently. “Do you know what the kingdom plans?” he asked. “A northern campaign. Twenty thousand soldiers through Bellweather Pass. Villages emptied for supplies. Fields burned. Sons buried in foreign earth.”

Mara had heard rumors of war, but nothing certain.

“I found the orders in the archive,” Edrin continued. “So I opened Nemor’s book and removed the road. No road, no campaign.”

“You removed four thousand people.”

“Temporarily.”

“They were being forgotten.”

“A necessary price.”

“To whom?”

His calm expression cracked. “You think ink is innocent? Every map in your Royal Room serves the throne. You draw roads, and armies march on them. You mark borders, and men die defending lines they cannot see. I did what cartographers always do. I changed the world with a pen.”

Mara looked at the book.

“Then put the road back,” she said. “Warn the villages. Block the pass another way.”

“I cannot.”

“Why not?”

“The book requires balance. To hide one road, it consumes every path connected to it. It began with milestones and maps. Then memories. Soon the region itself will disappear.”

“You knew this?”

“Not when I began.”

The tower trembled. One of the wall maps turned blank.

Edrin seized the book. “Help me control it. We can make a better kingdom. Erase roads to prisons. Erase the doors of tyrants. Remove borders.”

“And when the book asks for balance?”

He said nothing.

Mara drew her small knife.

Edrin smiled sadly. “You cannot cut a book that has forgotten fire and steel.”

She did not attack the book.

She cut her palm.

Then she pressed her bleeding hand onto a blank page.

“My name is Mara Venn,” she said. “My brother is Jonas Venn. Master Orin hates cinnamon tea but drinks it when he is worried. Alderhook grows pears. Saint Lume has two bells, and the western bell rings flat in winter.”

Black letters spread beneath her hand.

The book snapped shut.

Edrin lunged, but Mara held it against her chest. The room twisted. Roads appeared in the air around them: streets, footpaths, bridges, stairs, tunnels, all crossing one another in a shining web.

She understood then. Edrin had tried to command the book with geography. Nemor had sealed it with memory.

A road was not only a route between places.

It was the journey to a brother. The way home after grief. The path along which pears were carried, armies marched, strangers met, and promises returned.

Mara opened the book again.

Its pages were empty.

She began to draw the North Road.

Not perfectly. She included every bend she remembered and invented those she did not. She marked Alderhook and Saint Lume. She drew Bracken Ford, Quiet Valley, the Lantern Inn, and Bellweather Pass.

Beside the road, she wrote the names of people.

The tower shook violently.

“What are you doing?” Edrin cried.

“Giving the road back to those who use it.”

“You’ll restore the campaign!”

“Perhaps. Then we’ll stop it as people, not by erasing one another.”

The shining roads tightened around Edrin. He tried to run, but every path carried him back to the pedestal.

Mara drew one final line southward to the capital.

Then she rang Jonas’s brass bell.

The sound was small and clear.

The tower turned right side up.

Mara fell through the door into snow.

Behind her, Nemor’s Watch collapsed—not into stone, but into thousands of scraps of paper that whirled over the frozen lake. Edrin was gone. The white book lay at Mara’s feet, its cover now dark and ordinary.

She carried it south.

The road remained.

At Saint Lume, Jonas was waiting. At Alderhook, villagers loaded carts with pears. At the thirty-third mile, Master Orin stood with half the Royal Map Room, all of them holding maps covered in names.

His wife was beside him.

For several days, the kingdom struggled to remember itself. Families were reunited. Missing villages returned to tax ledgers. Signposts emerged from trees. The North Road reappeared on maps throughout the palace.

So did the king’s campaign plans.

Master Orin, however, had made copies of Edrin’s evidence. These reached the northern villages, the city guilds, and several members of the royal council. When the army assembled, it found the North Road crowded with thousands of unarmed citizens carrying maps on which the pass had been labeled:

NO ROAD TO WAR.

The soldiers refused to advance.

The campaign ended before it began.

Years later, Mara became Master of the Royal Map Room. She changed its rules.

Every official map still showed rivers, mountains, borders, and roads. But along the edges, cartographers added smaller truths.

Here an old woman gives water to travelers.

Here two sisters planted an oak after their quarrel.

Here soldiers turned back.

Here a river once ran.

The white book remained locked in a cabinet beneath Mara’s desk. She never opened it, though kings, ministers, and generals asked her to. Sometimes they demanded. Sometimes they threatened.

Mara always gave the same answer.

“A map may guide the world,” she told them, “but it must never be allowed to own it.”

And on quiet mornings, when sunlight fell across her desk, she painted the lost river in the western hills.

It had dried before she was born. No traveler would ever drink from it again.

Still, she drew it broad and silver, flowing all the way to the sea.
